title: Cross-Topic Revision — Maths4U Original

provenance.basis: Independent mixed-skill briefs; no examination question supplied for paraphrasing.

marking_policy: Maths4U indicative marking guidance, not an official examination-board mark scheme. Award stated criteria once each, up to the part maximum. Accept valid equivalent methods. Follow-through applies only where explicitly stated; do not award an accuracy criterion for an incorrect final result.

lessons.title: Quadratics, functions and admissible solutions
lessons.objective: Choose a useful quadratic form, retain a function domain and interpret every algebraic candidate.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: complete a square, find inverse/composite functions and use a discriminant.

Begin a mixed question by writing its domain. The completed-square form \(a(x-h)^2+k\) reveals a turning point and a range; the expanded form can be more useful for an intersection equation. Select the representation that exposes the next step.

A quadratic becomes invertible only on a suitable one-to-one domain. After swapping input and output, choose the square-root branch that returns values in the original domain. The inverse domain is the original range. For f(g(x)), require g(x) to belong to the domain of f before solving the equation.

A substitution or squaring step can produce algebraic candidates that fail these restrictions. Substitute candidates into the original question. For intersections giving a genuine quadratic, Δ>0 means two distinct real roots, Δ=0 a repeated root, and Δ<0 no real roots. A later domain restriction may reduce that count.

Recall later

Keep a short list: original domain, inverse branch, candidate roots, accepted roots. A valid algebraic root is not automatically a valid function input.

examples.question_html: For \(f(x)=(x+1)^2+2\), x≥−1, find the inverse and solve f(x)≤11.
examples.solution_html: The range is [2,∞), and \(f^{-1}(x)=-1+\sqrt{x-2}\) for x≥2. In the inequality, x+1≥0 and (x+1)²≤9, so −1≤x≤2.

examples.question_html: Let q(x)=(x−2)² for x≥2 and g(x)=3x+1. Solve q(g(x))=16.
examples.solution_html: The composition requires 3x+1≥2, or x≥1/3. The equation (3x−1)²=16 gives x=5/3 or −1. Only 5/3 satisfies the composition domain.

examples.question_html: How many intersections do y=x²+1 and y=mx+2 have for each real m?
examples.solution_html: The equation is x²−mx−1=0. Its discriminant is m²+4>0 for every real m, so there are always two distinct real intersections. No parameter value makes these two unrestricted graphs tangent.

common_mistakes: Taking both square-root branches for a restricted inverse.
Solving a composite equation before checking its domain.
Using the discriminant root count without applying the remaining restrictions.

lessons.title: Lines, circles and derivatives
lessons.objective: Connect tangent slopes, radius geometry and distance optimisation without losing special cases.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: differentiate polynomials, use line/circle equations and classify a global minimum.

A tangent to \(y=f(x)\) at \(P=(a,f(a))\) has finite slope \(f^{\prime}(a)\). A circle through P is tangent to that line when its radius CP is perpendicular to the line. For finite nonzero slopes the product is −1; horizontal/vertical pairs require a geometric statement instead of division by zero.

Substitution provides a second check: intersect the proposed line with the circle. A repeated solution at P confirms a single point of contact. Use the point coordinates in both original equations, not merely a matching slope.

For a nearest-point problem, write the squared distance \(Q(t)\). Since the square-root function is increasing on nonnegative numbers, minimising Q also minimises distance. Differentiate Q, retain the feasible parameters and justify a global result before taking the square root.

Recall later

A stationary squared distance is a candidate. Domain endpoints and the derivative sign pattern decide whether it is the closest point.

examples.question_html: Find a circle centred at (3,0) that shares the tangent to \(y=x^2\) at (1,1).
examples.solution_html: The tangent is \(y=2x-1\). The radius vector is \((-2,1)\), so its slope is \(-1/2\) and its squared length is 5. The circle is \((x-3)^2+y^2=5\). Substituting the tangent gives \(5(x-1)^2=0\), confirming contact at (1,1).

examples.question_html: Find the point \((t,t^2)\), t≥0, closest to A(0,1).
examples.solution_html: \(Q=t^2+(t^2-1)^2\), so \(Q=t^4-t^2+1\). Its derivative is \(2t(2t^2-1)\), negative before \(1/\sqrt2\) and positive afterwards on the positive domain. The closest point is \((1/\sqrt2,1/2)\), with \(Q=3/4\) and distance \(\sqrt3/2\). The endpoint gives the larger distance 1.

examples.question_html: Find the tangent and normal at the vertex of \(y=(x-2)^2+4\), and a circle centred at (2,1) sharing that tangent.
examples.solution_html: At (2,4), the tangent is \(y=4\) and the normal is \(x=2\). The radius from (2,1) is vertical with length 3, so the circle \((x-2)^2+(y-1)^2=9\) has the same horizontal tangent. No numerical reciprocal of zero is needed.

common_mistakes: Checking a slope but not whether the point lies on both curves.
Forgetting that a horizontal tangent has a vertical normal.
Reporting the minimum squared distance as the distance, or ignoring the feasible parameter range.

lessons.title: Trigonometric branches and sector models
lessons.objective: Carry all permitted angles into radian geometry, then optimise only within the valid sector model.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: solve trigonometric equations on an interval, use radians and differentiate a quadratic.

For radius r and angle θ in radians, arc length is rθ and sector area is r²θ/2. For 0<θ<π, the triangle formed by the radii has area r²sin θ/2, so the minor-segment area is r²(θ−sin θ)/2. An equation in sine can give two angles on that interval, with different sector areas.

For a proper sector with two distinct radial edges, perimeter P=rθ+2r. This boundary description uses 0<θ<2π; at a full turn the two radial edges no longer form an ordinary external sector boundary. State the valid range before eliminating θ.

If P is fixed, substitute θ=P/r−2 into the area to obtain \(A=Pr/2-r^2\). This quadratic is easy to differentiate. The stationary radius is useful only if its angle and radius satisfy the sector constraints. A completed-square bound or full derivative-sign argument proves global optimality.

Recall later

Find all admissible angles first. Equal sine values do not imply equal radian angles, arc lengths or sector areas.

examples.question_html: A circle has radius 4. The triangle formed by two radii has area 4 and 0<θ<π. Find θ and the corresponding sector areas.
examples.solution_html: 8sin θ=4 gives θ=π/6 or 5π/6. The sector area is 8θ, giving 4π/3 or 20π/3 respectively. The two angle branches must remain matched to their own areas.

examples.question_html: Find the minor-segment area for radius 4 and angle π/3.
examples.solution_html: The sector area is 8π/3; the triangle area is 8sin(π/3)=4√3. Their difference is 8π/3−4√3 square units.

examples.question_html: A proper sector has perimeter 16. Find its greatest area.
examples.solution_html: θ=16/r−2 and A=8r−r², with 8/(1+π)<r<8. A′=8−2r gives r=4, θ=2. Since A=16−(r−4)², the feasible candidate gives the global maximum 16 square units.

common_mistakes: Using degrees in the arc or sector formulas.
Keeping only the principal sine angle.
Optimising an algebraic expression without checking that its radius and angle describe the stated sector.

lessons.title: Coefficients as sequence data
lessons.objective: Extract coefficients before imposing a progression condition, then justify signs and integer thresholds.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: expand a positive integer power and use arithmetic/geometric progression formulas.

The coefficient of xʲ in (1+kx)ⁿ is \(\binom nj k^j\). It is a number once k is fixed; the term also includes xʲ. If coefficients form a progression, use the numbers, not expressions still containing x. The constant coefficient is 1.

For three consecutive arithmetic terms u,v,w, use 2v=u+w. For a geometric progression, use a finite common-ratio recurrence; for nonzero terms this implies v²=uw. An even-power coefficient can leave two parameter signs or branches, which the stated progression conditions must resolve.

For a nonzero first term a, an infinite GP sum needs |r|<1 and equals a/(1−r). Its signed tail after n terms is arⁿ/(1−r); use the absolute tail for an error tolerance. A strict threshold needs an integer n and a check at the preceding index. A binomial index starts at zero, while GP term numbers start at one.

Recall later

Separate the algebraic step from the sequence step: coefficient equation → admissible parameter → progression formula → integer/domain check.

examples.question_html: Use the x and x² coefficients of (1+2x)^4 as the first two AP terms. Find the sum of its first five terms.
examples.solution_html: The coefficients are 8 and 24, so a=8 and d=16. The fifth term is 72 and \(S_5=5(8+72)/2=200\).

examples.question_html: The x² coefficient of (1+rx)^4 is 3/2, with 0<r<1. A GP has first term 3 and ratio r. Find its infinite sum.
examples.solution_html: 6r²=3/2 gives r²=1/4. The stated range selects r=1/2. The GP converges and its sum is 3/(1−1/2)=6.

examples.question_html: A GP has a=5 and r=2/3. Find the least positive integer n for which the omitted tail is less than 1.
examples.solution_html: The infinite sum is 15 and the tail is 15(2/3)ⁿ. At n=6 it is 320/243>1; at n=7 it is 640/729<1. The positive tails decrease strictly, so the least index is 7.

common_mistakes: Using polynomial terms instead of coefficients as progression data.
Selecting a sign merely because the coefficient was squared.
Treating a noninteger threshold as a term count or using an infinite sum without checking the ratio.

lessons.title: Recovered curves, regions and accumulated quantities
lessons.objective: Link integration and differentiation while distinguishing an area, a volume and the growth of an accumulated value.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: recover a curve from a gradient, find intersections, integrate regions and use derivative signs.

Recover the curve and its constant before using its ordinate in another model. To find a bounded area, identify the intersections and integrate upper minus lower. For a rotation, draw the same region relative to the axis and use squared disk or washer radii instead. These are different quantities with different units.

If \(V(k)=\pi\int_a^k R(x)^2\,dx\), then at interior k, V′(k)=πR(k)². This derivative is cross-sectional area: volume per unit length, not a time rate. Where it is positive, V grows. Its greatest growth need not occur at the largest V. Check endpoints when maximising either quantity.

For a time-rate model, integrate the rate and add the initial amount. A zero rate locates a candidate extremum of the amount; its sign pattern and the allowed time interval establish the global result.

Recall later

Label the target before calculating: curve, gradient, area, volume, amount or rate. Keep units with the final target.

examples.question_html: A curve has y′=4x−4 and y(0)=5. Find its stationary point and the area enclosed with y=5.
examples.solution_html: The curve is y=2x²−4x+5, with minimum (1,3). The line meets it at 0 and 2. Its enclosed area is ∫₀²(4x−2x²)dx=8/3 square units. Rotation about the x-axis would instead use π∫₀²(25−y²)dx.

examples.question_html: For 0≤k≤1, let \(V(k)=\pi\int_0^k(1-x)^2\,dx\). Compare where the disk area and total volume are largest.
examples.solution_html: V(k)=π(k−k²+k³/3). Disk area π(1−k)² is largest at k=0, while V increases over the interval and is largest at k=1, with value π/3. The largest cross-section and largest accumulated volume answer different questions.

examples.question_html: An amount has rate 8−4t and initial value 6 on 0≤t≤3. Find its greatest and final values.
examples.solution_html: Q(t)=6+8t−2t²=14−2(t−2)². Its greatest value is 14 at t=2, which is feasible. The final value is Q(3)=12; the rate has already become negative, but the net change is still +6.

common_mistakes: Using the gradient instead of the recovered ordinate in an area or volume.
Squaring a vertical separation instead of subtracting squared washer radii.
Confusing the maximum accumulated value with its maximum rate or omitting a feasible endpoint.

problems.title: A restricted inverse and a composite equation
problems.objective: Combine a completed square, an inverse branch, a composition domain and an inequality.
problems.stem_html: Let \(f(x)=2(x-1)^2+5\) for x≥1, and let \(g(x)=3x-2\) for real x.
problems.hint_html: The outer function accepts inputs at least 1. Use that condition before accepting roots of the composite equation.

parts.prompt_html: Find the range of f and its inverse, including the inverse domain.
parts.solution_html: For x≥1, x−1≥0 and f has minimum 5. Solving y=2(x−1)²+5 gives x−1=√((y−5)/2), choosing the nonnegative branch. Hence the displayed inverse has input domain [5,∞) and output range [1,∞).

criteria.requirement: Give the range [5,∞).
Give the correct positive-branch inverse.
State its domain x≥5, consistent with the original range.

parts.alternative_methods: An equivalent exact square-root expression is accepted.
parts.common_error: Keeping both square-root branches or confusing the two domains.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Solve \(f(g(x))=23\), retaining only valid inputs.
parts.solution_html: The composition requires 3x−2≥1, so x≥1. The equation becomes 2(3x−3)²+5=23, hence (3x−3)²=9. Its algebraic candidates are x=0 and x=2. Only x=2 satisfies the composition domain; direct substitution gives f(g(2))=f(4)=23.

criteria.requirement: Obtain composition domain x≥1.
Find both algebraic candidates 0 and 2.
Retain only x=2 with a valid domain check.

parts.alternative_methods: Using the inverse f⁻¹(23)=4 and then solving g(x)=4 is accepted.
parts.common_error: Accepting the discarded square-root branch as a composition solution.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find all permitted x such that f(x)≤13.
parts.solution_html: The inequality gives (x−1)²≤4. Together with x≥1 this becomes 0≤x−1≤2, or 1≤x≤3. Equivalently the increasing branch runs from its vertex to f⁻¹(13)=3.

criteria.requirement: Solve the quadratic inequality with the stated branch restriction.
Give the complete closed interval [1,3].

parts.alternative_methods: Monotonicity and inverse-endpoint reasoning is accepted.
parts.common_error: Giving the unrestricted interval [−1,3].
parts.label: c

problems.title: A line parameter controls intersection count
problems.objective: Connect a quadratic discriminant with tangent lines and their contact points.
problems.stem_html: Consider the parabola \(y=x^2-4x+7\) and the family of lines \(y=mx+3\), with m real.
problems.hint_html: Eliminate y first. A repeated intersection root identifies a tangent contact, whose coordinates still need to be found.

parts.prompt_html: Form the quadratic equation for the x-coordinates of intersections.
parts.solution_html: Equating the ordinates gives x²−4x+7=mx+3. Collecting terms gives x²−(m+4)x+4=0.

criteria.requirement: Equate the original curve and line.
Obtain the complete intersection quadratic.

parts.alternative_methods: An equivalent rearrangement is accepted.
parts.common_error: Dropping the line constant or giving an equation only in m.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find all m for which there are two distinct real intersection points.
parts.solution_html: The discriminant is (m+4)²−16. Requiring it to be strictly positive gives |m+4|>4, hence m<−8 or m>0. At the excluded boundary values the intersection is repeated.

criteria.requirement: Use the correct discriminant with a strict positive condition.
Solve both outside branches of the inequality.
Give m<−8 or m>0 with boundary values excluded.

parts.alternative_methods: Factor m(m+8)>0 and use a sign chart.
parts.common_error: Including tangency by using a non-strict inequality.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find both tangent lines in this family and their points of contact.
parts.solution_html: Discriminant zero gives m=0 or −8. The repeated root is x=(m+4)/2. For m=0 it is 2, with y=3. For m=−8 it is −2, with y=19. The parabola derivative 2x−4 agrees with each stated line slope.

criteria.requirement: Find both parameter values 0 and −8.
Give tangent y=3 and contact (2,3).
Give tangent y=−8x+3 and contact (−2,19).

parts.alternative_methods: Solve the derivative slope condition together with the point lying on the corresponding line.
parts.common_error: Giving the parameter values without line equations and contact points.
parts.label: c

problems.title: One tangent shared by two curves
problems.objective: Combine a polynomial derivative, a circle equation and a repeated intersection test.
problems.stem_html: The point P=(2,2) lies on the parabola \(y=x^2-2x+2\). A circle has centre C=(4,1) and passes through P.
problems.hint_html: Use the derivative for the parabola, distance for the circle, and substitution for a separate tangency check.

parts.prompt_html: Find the tangent to the parabola at P.
parts.solution_html: The derivative is 2x−2, so its value at x=2 is 2. The tangent through (2,2) is y−2=2(x−2), hence y=2x−2.

criteria.requirement: Find the derivative 2x−2.
Use slope 2 and the point P.
Give the correct tangent equation.

parts.alternative_methods: A first-principles derivative is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using the ordinate as a slope without differentiating the curve.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the equation of the circle.
parts.solution_html: The squared radius is CP²=(2−4)²+(2−1)²=5. With centre (4,1), the equation is (x−4)²+(y−1)²=5.

criteria.requirement: Find the squared radius 5.
Give the correct circle equation.

parts.alternative_methods: An equivalent expanded circle equation is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using 5 as the radius and squaring it again.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: By substituting the line from (a) into the circle equation, prove that it is also tangent to the circle at P.
parts.answer_html: The equation reduces to \(5(x-2)^2=0\), giving only P.
parts.solution_html: Substituting y=2x−2 gives (x−4)²+(2x−3)²=5. Expanding reduces it to 5x²−20x+20=5(x−2)²=0. Thus x=2 is the only, repeated root and the line gives y=2. The unique circle contact is P, so the line is tangent there.

criteria.requirement: Substitute the correct line into the circle.
Obtain the repeated-root equation 5(x−2)²=0.
Identify the unique point P and conclude tangency.

parts.alternative_methods: An equivalent substitution followed by a zero discriminant is accepted.
parts.common_error: Asserting that the parabola tangent is automatically a circle tangent without checking the circle.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A nearest point and its normal
problems.objective: Minimise squared distance on a restricted curve and check the geometric normal condition.
problems.stem_html: A point P=(x,x²), with x≥0, moves on the parabola y=x². The fixed point is A=(0,3).
problems.hint_html: Minimise AP² before taking a square root. Explain why the chosen stationary value gives the global minimum.

parts.prompt_html: Express the squared distance Q=AP² as a polynomial in x.
parts.solution_html: Q=(x−0)²+(x²−3)²=x²+x⁴−6x²+9=x⁴−5x²+9.

criteria.requirement: Use both coordinate differences in the distance-squared formula.
Expand to x⁴−5x²+9.

parts.alternative_methods: An equivalent factored distance expression with the correct expansion is accepted.
parts.common_error: Minimising only the vertical separation.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the point P for which AP is least and justify the global result.
parts.solution_html: Q′=4x³−10x=2x(2x²−5). For positive x it is negative before √(5/2) and positive afterwards. Hence Q decreases from the boundary x=0, then increases after the unique interior minimum. The nearest point has x=√(5/2)=√10/2 and y=5/2. Minimising Q minimises AP since the square root is increasing.

criteria.requirement: Differentiate and obtain the feasible positive stationary input √(5/2).
Give the corresponding point (√10/2,5/2).
Justify a global minimum on x≥0 and the use of squared distance.

parts.alternative_methods: Use Q=(x²−5/2)²+11/4 as a global bound, with its equality value feasible.
parts.common_error: Selecting the stationary boundary x=0 without comparing behaviour or ignoring x≥0.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the least distance AP and show that AP is normal to the parabola there.
parts.answer_html: Least distance \(\sqrt{11}/2\); AP slope \(-1/\sqrt{10}\), tangent slope \(\sqrt{10}\).
parts.solution_html: At the point, Q=5/2+(−1/2)²=11/4, so AP=√11/2. The line AP has slope (5/2−3)/(√10/2)=−1/√10. The parabola tangent slope is 2x=√10; their product is −1, proving AP is normal.

criteria.requirement: Give the distance √11/2 rather than its square.
Find the joining-line and tangent slopes correctly.
Use their product −1 to conclude perpendicularity.

parts.alternative_methods: A zero dot product of direction vectors is accepted.
parts.common_error: Reporting 11/4 as the distance or checking perpendicularity at a different point.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Two angles with one triangle area
problems.objective: Keep both sine branches and carry the correct radian angle into a segment calculation.
problems.stem_html: Two radii of a circle of radius 6 cm enclose an angle θ with 0<θ<π radians. The triangle formed by the radii and their chord has area 9 cm².
problems.hint_html: The triangle area uses sin θ, whereas the sector area uses θ itself. Keep the two angle branches separate.

parts.prompt_html: Find all possible θ exactly.
parts.solution_html: The triangle area is (1/2)(6²)sin θ=18sin θ. Thus sin θ=1/2. On the stated interval both π/6 and 5π/6 are permitted.

criteria.requirement: Form 18sin θ=9.
Obtain sin θ=1/2.
Give both and only permitted exact radian angles.

parts.alternative_methods: A unit-circle or reference-angle argument is accepted.
parts.common_error: Keeping only the inverse-calculator principal angle.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the corresponding sector area for each angle.
parts.solution_html: The sector area is 18θ. It gives 18(π/6)=3π cm² and 18(5π/6)=15π cm². The equal triangle areas do not make the sectors equal.

criteria.requirement: Use the radian sector formula and obtain 3π cm² for the smaller angle.
Obtain 15π cm² for the larger angle with correct matching.

parts.alternative_methods: Equivalent exact expressions are accepted.
parts.common_error: Putting sin θ into the sector formula.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: For the larger angle, find the minor-segment area exactly.
parts.solution_html: The larger angle 5π/6 is still less than π, so this is a minor segment. Subtract its triangle from its sector: S=18(θ−sin θ)=15π−9 cm².

criteria.requirement: Identify sector minus the enclosed triangle as the segment area.
Use the larger permitted angle and its matching triangle area.
Give 15π−9 cm².

parts.alternative_methods: Subtracting the known triangle area directly from 15π is accepted.
parts.common_error: Subtracting the small-angle sector or adding the triangle area.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A sector constraint becomes a quadratic
problems.objective: Convert a proper-sector perimeter into an area model and prove a feasible global optimum.
problems.stem_html: A proper circular sector has radius r>0 cm and central angle 0<θ<2π radians. Its boundary consists of two distinct radii and the connecting arc, with total length 20 cm.
problems.hint_html: Eliminate θ and use r as the optimisation variable. The proper-sector angle range imposes an extra lower bound on r.

parts.prompt_html: Express θ and the sector area A in terms of r, and state the feasible interval for r.
parts.solution_html: The perimeter equation is rθ+2r=20, so θ=20/r−2. Then A=r²θ/2=10r−r². The inequalities 0<20/r−2<2π, with r>0, give 10/(1+π)<r<10. Both boundaries are excluded.

criteria.requirement: Obtain θ=20/r−2.
Obtain A=10r−r².
Give the complete strict radius interval.

parts.alternative_methods: Use r=20/(θ+2) to derive the equivalent constraints before expressing the requested model in r.
parts.common_error: Using only r<10 or including a full-turn boundary.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Use differentiation to find the greatest sector area, stating the corresponding r and θ and justifying global optimality.
parts.solution_html: A′=10−2r vanishes at r=5. It gives θ=20/5−2=2 and A=25. The candidate is feasible because 0<2<2π. Also A=25−(r−5)²≤25 on the entire feasible domain, with equality at r=5, so this is the global maximum.

criteria.requirement: Differentiate and find the feasible candidate r=5 with θ=2.
Give the greatest area 25 cm².
Justify the global result and admissibility on the stated domain.

parts.alternative_methods: A complete derivative-sign or concavity argument on the feasible interval is accepted.
parts.common_error: Keeping an algebraic stationary point without checking the sector angle.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: When θ=π/2 instead, find r and A exactly.
parts.solution_html: The perimeter gives r=20/(2+π/2)=40/(4+π). The area is r²π/4=400π/(4+π)² cm². This angle is feasible but differs from the optimal angle 2 rad.

criteria.requirement: Give the exact radius 40/(4+π).
Give the exact sector area 400π/(4+π)² cm².

parts.alternative_methods: Substitution into A=10r−r² is accepted if simplified to an equivalent exact result.
parts.common_error: Using π/2 degrees or changing the perimeter model when the angle changes.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Binomial coefficients in an arithmetic progression
problems.objective: Turn a coefficient condition into a quadratic, then select a parameter using the direction of a progression.
problems.stem_html: In the expansion of \((1+kx)^6\), with k real, the coefficients of x⁰, x¹ and x², in that order, form three consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression.
problems.hint_html: The sequence uses coefficients, not the polynomial terms. An increasing progression requires a positive common difference.

parts.prompt_html: Show that k satisfies \(15k^2-12k+1=0\).
parts.solution_html: The first three coefficients are 1, 6k and 15k². Twice the middle AP term equals the sum of the outer terms, so 12k=1+15k², giving the stated quadratic.

criteria.requirement: Extract the three correct coefficient values.
Use the AP relation between them.
Obtain 15k²−12k+1=0.

parts.alternative_methods: Equating successive differences is accepted.
parts.common_error: Including x and x² in the progression data or using a GP product condition.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find both possible k exactly.
parts.solution_html: The quadratic formula gives k=(12±√(144−60))/30=(12±2√21)/30=(6±√21)/15. Both are real and both are positive, so positivity alone cannot select a branch.

criteria.requirement: Use the quadratic formula or complete the square correctly.
Give both exact roots (6±√21)/15.

parts.alternative_methods: Equivalent exact surd expressions are accepted.
parts.common_error: Rejecting a branch without using the remaining condition.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: It is now given that the progression is increasing. Select k and find the common difference exactly.
parts.solution_html: The difference is d=6k−1=(7±2√21)/5. Since 2√21>7, the minus branch has negative difference and the plus branch positive difference. Increasing order therefore selects the plus value of k and d=(7+2√21)/5.

criteria.requirement: Express the common difference using the coefficient values.
Select the plus parameter branch using the sign of the difference.
Give the exact difference (7+2√21)/5 with the rejected branch correctly accounted for.

parts.alternative_methods: Compare both pairs of consecutive coefficients directly.
parts.common_error: Selecting the plus branch solely because k must be positive; both roots are positive.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A coefficient determines a convergent ratio
problems.objective: Combine an even binomial coefficient with convergence data and a strict integer-tail bound.
problems.stem_html: A GP has first term a>0, ratio 0<r<1 and infinite sum 12. The coefficient of x² in \((1+rx)^5\) is 5/2.
problems.hint_html: The ratio restriction selects a root of the coefficient equation. For the final part, compare tails at consecutive integer indices.

parts.prompt_html: Find r and a.
parts.solution_html: The coefficient is 10r²=5/2, so r²=1/4. Since 0<r<1, r=1/2. From a/(1−r)=12 we get a=6.

criteria.requirement: Use the correct binomial coefficient equation.
Select r=1/2 using the given ratio domain.
Use the infinite sum to obtain a=6.

parts.alternative_methods: Equivalent elimination using the convergent GP formula is accepted.
parts.common_error: Keeping the negative ratio root despite the stated positive domain.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the first-four-term sum and the omitted tail after those four terms.
parts.solution_html: S_4=6(1−(1/2)⁴)/(1−1/2)=12(15/16)=45/4. Subtracting from the infinite sum gives 12−45/4=3/4.

criteria.requirement: Give the exact finite sum 45/4.
Give the distinct omitted tail 3/4.

parts.alternative_methods: Adding 6+3+3/2+3/4 directly is accepted.
parts.common_error: Treating the fourth term as the whole omitted tail.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the least positive integer n for which the omitted tail is less than 0.02.
parts.solution_html: The tail is R_n=12·2⁻ⁿ. Requiring R_n<1/50 gives 2ⁿ>600. At n=9 the tail is 3/128≈0.0234375, while at n=10 it is 3/256≈0.01171875. The tails decrease strictly, so the least successful n is 10.

criteria.requirement: Form the correct strict tail inequality.
Obtain n=10.
Check the consecutive bounds and justify minimality.

parts.alternative_methods: A logarithm calculation followed by a valid strict integer check is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using an individual term threshold or rounding a real index down.
parts.label: c

problems.title: One recovered curve, two geometric quantities
problems.objective: Connect a gradient condition, a stationary point, enclosed area and washer volume.
problems.stem_html: A curve has \(dy/dx=6x-6\) for real x and passes through (0,8). Coordinates are measured in cm.
problems.hint_html: Recover y first. For the enclosed region, the horizontal line is above a positive curve, so the area and rotated volume use different integrands.

parts.prompt_html: Find the curve equation and its stationary point, stating the nature of the point.
parts.solution_html: Integration gives y=3x²−6x+C, with C=8 from the point. The derivative vanishes at x=1, where y=5. The second derivative is 6>0, so this is a minimum.

criteria.requirement: Recover the complete curve using the point condition.
Find the stationary point (1,5).
Classify a minimum with a valid derivative or completed-square argument.

parts.alternative_methods: Write y=3(x−1)²+5 to confirm the classification.
parts.common_error: Using the given gradient itself as the curve ordinate.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the area enclosed by the curve and the line y=8.
parts.solution_html: Intersections satisfy 3x²−6x+8=8, giving x=0 and 2. On (0,2), the line is above the curve. Thus A=∫₀²(6x−3x²)dx=[3x²−x³]₀²=4 cm².

criteria.requirement: Find both intersections 0 and 2 and the correct upper curve.
Set up the area as upper minus lower.
Evaluate 4 cm².

parts.alternative_methods: A complete symmetric area calculation is accepted.
parts.common_error: Integrating the curve alone instead of the vertical separation.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: The enclosed region is rotated about the x-axis. Find its volume exactly.
parts.solution_html: The outer radius is 8 and inner radius y=3x²−6x+8, which is at least 5. The washer integral is π∫₀²{64−(3x²−6x+8)²}dx. Its integrand expands to −9x⁴+36x³−84x²+96x. The integral is π{−288/5+144−224+192}=272π/5 cm³.

criteria.requirement: Use the correct squared outer and inner radii over [0,2].
Expand and integrate the washer expression correctly.
Give 272π/5 cm³ exactly.

parts.alternative_methods: Subtract the inner solid volume from the enclosing cylinder volume.
parts.common_error: Squaring the area integrand (8−y) instead of using 64−y².
parts.label: c

problems.title: The largest volume and its fastest growth
problems.objective: Use a polynomial radius, integrate to a variable boundary and distinguish a quantity from its derivative.
problems.stem_html: For 0≤k≤4, the region under \(y=x(4-x)\) between x=0 and x=k is rotated about the x-axis. Coordinates are in cm and the resulting volume is V(k).
problems.hint_html: Square the radius before integrating. The derivative with respect to the cut-off coordinate k measures cross-sectional area, not elapsed time.

parts.prompt_html: Find an explicit expression for V(k).
parts.solution_html: The radius is nonnegative on [0,4]. Its square is x²(4−x)²=16x²−8x³+x⁴. Hence V(k)=π∫₀ᵏ(16x²−8x³+x⁴)dx=π(16k³/3−2k⁴+k⁵/5). The lower limit fixes V(0)=0.

criteria.requirement: Expand the squared radius as 16x²−8x³+x⁴.
Integrate every term correctly.
Evaluate the variable limits and retain π without a free constant.

parts.alternative_methods: An equivalent exact antiderivative expression evaluated from 0 to k is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using the unsquared profile or introducing an arbitrary volume constant.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the volume when k=4 exactly.

criteria.requirement: Substitute the upper cut-off 4 into the complete expression.
Give 512π/15 cm³ exactly.

parts.alternative_methods: A separate definite integral of the squared radius over [0,4] is accepted.
parts.common_error: Rounding intermediate fractions or omitting π.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find where V grows most rapidly with respect to k, including the greatest growth value. Explain why this differs from where V is greatest.
parts.answer_html: Greatest \(V^{\prime}=16\pi\) cm² at k=2 cm; V itself is greatest at k=4 cm.
parts.solution_html: V′(k)=πk²(4−k)² is the disk area. Its derivative is 4πk(k−2)(k−4), positive for 0<k<2 and negative for 2<k<4. With endpoint values zero, the global maximum disk area is V′(2)=16π cm². However V′ is positive throughout (0,4), so V is strictly increasing and its greatest value occurs at k=4. This is growth per unit length, not a time rate.

criteria.requirement: Identify V′(k) as πk²(4−k)².
Find the maximum-growth candidate k=2 with valid differentiation or an equivalent bound.
Give the global greatest growth value 16π cm² with endpoint/sign reasoning.
Explain that V remains increasing and therefore is greatest at k=4.

parts.alternative_methods: Bound the nonnegative radius by 4 using x(4−x)=4−(x−2)², then distinguish the accumulated volume.
parts.common_error: Claiming V is largest at k=2 because its derivative is largest there.
parts.label: c
